replying_to: Replying to Learning to Coordinate in Multi-Agent Systems: A Coordinated Actor-Critic Algorithm and Finite-Time Guarantees
display_title: Official Review of Paper2237 by Reviewer 2aty

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper introduces a new class of multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms in which the agent's policy parameters are decomposed into two parts; one part which is shared across (neighbouring) agents and another which is optimised only by the agent. The motivation of the paper is to leverage the benefit of the existing extremes (full sharing among homogenous agents and totally localised updates). The paper then proves some results on finite-time bounds as well as performing a simple empirical analysis.
content.main_review:
Parameter sharing and communication serve as useful tools to speed up and stabilise learning in multi-agent systems and even improve overall outcomes. However, in some situations forcing the agents to share all parameters and use some common updating procedure such as consensus updates on their learning parameters may be inappropriate; therefore allowing the agents to have some individual component of their learning update would seemingly be beneficial in some circumstances. This is somewhat achieved by allowing the agents to jointly estimate a global value functions while individually optimising their local policies. The idea of this paper seems novel in that it pushes this question one step further allowing the agents to have both an individual and a shared component of their policy parameter. 

Though I found the idea quite novel, the paper seems to have several gaps which make it i) very difficult to understand the idea in its entirety ii) hard to evaluate the benefits relative to existing approaches iii) difficult to know whether the idea has practical benefit.

Specifically:

The paper has some nice theoretical results but omits any discussion about how the results improve the existing state of affairs. For example, for Theorem 1 it would have been nice to have a discussion about how this result compares to similar results for which there is not decoupling between shared and not-shared policy parameters. 

Proposition 1 seems to relate purely to the analysis of using linear approximations for the value functions and the global reward function. Given that linear approximation is a fairly common technique across RL in general, I think this needs a discussion to place these results in context with known results.

Also, I find the experiments to be quite weak. Though there are comparisons between the variants introduce in this paper (and some nice insights), no comparison to existing methods is performed and so one can’t evaluate the practical advantages over existing methods (this is also omitted in the theoretical analyses of the paper too).

Lastly, I didn't get a full sense of how the each decomposition formed i.e. learning what is best for the agents to share and what is best for them to keep localised. In other words, I couldn't see how each of the agent's two parameters affects the policy given that now the agent’s policy is determined by both parameters. The variants cover the two other extremes but I didn't get a feel of how the two parameters determine the agent's policy.

Lastly, there are a few restrictive assumptions in the paper. Though the references are convincing enough of the idea that these assumptions are common in some other works, it would be nice to include a brief discussion on the implications of these assumptions i.e. when will they hold true or be violated.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I found the idea novel and the paper has some useful theoretical analysis. However, there were some gaps (in the analyses and the empirical studies) which make it hard for me to understand how practicable the method is in its current form. Additionally, I think the paper is lacking discussions on how the results fit within the context of existing results. Since the benefits of the method haven't been backed up by empirical evaluation either the extent of the advantages of the method remain mainly unknown.

content.title: Response: Contributions and Clarifications
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the detailed review of the paper and the valuable feedback. Below, we address the reviewer's comments in a point-by-point manner.

**Your comment: The paper has some nice theoretical results but omits any discussion about how the results improve the existing state of affairs. For example, for Theorem 1 it would have been nice to have a discussion about how this result compares to similar results for which there is not decoupling between shared and not-shared policy parameters.**

**Our response:** Thank you for your comment. Below we restate the contribution of Theorem 1. 

As already pointed out in the “contribution” subsection of Sec. 1, our work is the first work that provides sample complexity bounds for actor-critic methods in this cooperative and decentralized MARL setting. When the policy is fully personalized, the setting is the same as [Zhang et al., 2018], the no finite-time analysis of which has not been tackled before our work. After the submission of this work, we found that there is a concurrent work [Chen et al., 2021], also submitted to ICLR 2022, which analyzes a related but different MARL algorithm (to be discussed in the following response).

When the policy is fully shared, the setting is new and there is no finite sample analysis available. We notice that there is a concurrent work [Communication-Efficient Actor-Critic Methods for Homogeneous Markov Games] also submitted to ICLR 2022, which considers the fully shared case of decentralized actor-critic algorithm for homogeneous Markov games. They only prove the asymptotic convergence guarantee. 

Regarding comparison with the centralized algorithms, our finite sample analysis matches the results in [Wu et al., 2020] which showed the sample complexity for standard two-timescale single-agent AC method is $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{−2.5})$. Moreover, there is a recent line of work that shows that a variant of single-agent AC can achieve $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{−2})$ complexity; see [Xu et al., 2020]. However, unlike the standard two-timescale AC algorithm, this algorithm requires large-batch samples / inner loops to perform TD steps before updating the actor each time. [Chen et al., 2021] mentioned in the previous paragraph extends this work to the decentralized MARL setting. To be specific, $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{−1} \ln \epsilon^{-1})$ samples need to be generated to update critic parameter before performing each actor update. While simple to analyze, these algorithms are not efficient in practice. In experiments, it can be observed that  this large-batch variant suffers from a poor sample complexity; further, since the agents need to wait a very long time between two policy updates (to collect enough samples for critics update), the runtime is high. In our revised version, we have included the comparison with this large-batch algorithm in numerical experiments. 

**Your comment: Proposition 1 seems to relate purely to the analysis of using linear approximations for the value functions and the global reward function. Given that linear approximation is a fairly common technique across RL in general, I think this needs a discussion to place these results in context with known results.**

**Our response:** Thank you. We agree that linear approximation is fairly common. We have revised our paper to present the following discussion after Proposition 1. 

In Proposition 1, under the linear approximations, we analyze the convergence rate of the approximators of the value function and the global reward function in decentralized two-timescale AC methods. Compared with existing works ([Wai et al., 2018] and [Doan et al., 2019]) which established finite-time convergence guarantees for decentralized policy evaluation problems under the fixed policy, our results in Proposition 1 are analyzed in a more challenging situation where both policies and critics are updated in a single loop / two-timescale scheme. Hence, the convergence of critics (the approximators of the value function and the global reward function) will be slowed down due to the convergence errors in policy parameters.

content.title: Response Continued: Contributions and Clarifications
content.comment:
**Your comment: Also, I find the experiments to be quite weak. Though there are comparisons between the variants introduce in this paper (and some nice insights), no comparison to existing methods is performed and so one can’t evaluate the practical advantages over existing methods (this is also omitted in the theoretical analyses of the paper too).**

**Our response:** Thanks for this question. To address your question, we have updated our paper by: 1) comparing the performance of CAC with benchmarks, for our pursuit-evasion game;  2) including one more experiment  (i.e., the coordination game) and comparing CAC with a few benchmarks. More specifically, We compare our algorithm CAC with independent AC, decentralized AC [Zhang et al., 2018] and the concurrent work mini-batch decentralized AC [Chen et al., 2021]. Please see Section 5 “Numerical Results”, the blue parts.

In summary, we conclude the numerical results and findings as below: 
* In the coordination game, we show that CAC provides faster convergence and has larger chances of converging to efficient equilibriums;
* In the pursuit-evasion game, we show CAC could achieve the fastest convergence speed compared with the benchmarks; 
* The proposed CAC algorithm has the potential benefits to learn the similarity and homogeneity among different local agents / tasks from the (partial) policy sharing scheme.

**Your comment: Lastly, I didn't get a full sense of how the each decomposition formed i.e. learning what is best for the agents to share and what is best for them to keep localised. In other words, I couldn't see how each of the agent's two parameters affects the policy given that now the agent’s policy is determined by both parameters. The variants cover the two other extremes but I didn't get a feel of how the two parameters determine the agent's policy.**

**Our response:** Thank you for your comment. We use the partial policy sharing only for generality, to cover the full spectrum of strategies ranging from no sharing to full sharing. 

(1) Partial policy sharing has been proven useful in a few popular settings; for example the personalized federated learning and the multi-task RL setting mentioned in the paper. Generally speaking, partial sharing is useful when local tasks / agents share some similarity. But it is true that besides the above intuition, there is no definite answer as to *when* to use the partial sharing. 
Further, in practice, when partial sharing is used, it is typically found useful to construct neural networks where the parameters of base layers (first few layers) are shared among different agents and the parameters of personalization layers (last few layers) are locally optimized for adapting to the statistical heterogeneity of the local tasks.

(2) To further address the question *how* to use partial sharing, below we provide a few examples:

In [Arivazhagan et al., 2019], a federated learning algorithm is developed to train the base layers (first few layers) through using existing decentralized optimization techniques to learn the similarities among different local datasets. Moreover, the personalization layers (last few layers) are trained locally to enable the neural network models to capture personalization information of local agents.

In [Yu et al., 2020], a multi-headed policy with one head per task is trained by the soft actor-critic algorithm in multi-task reinforcement learning environments. The policy is constructed by a neural network where the base layers are shared among different tasks and the personalized layers (heads) will adapt to each individual task.

Additionally, in our pursuit-evasion game experiments, the policy of each agent is constructed by a convolutional neural network. Each agent will share the parameters in convolutional layers with neighboring agents and locally optimize the parameters in the last layer (fully connected layer). In the coordination game, softmax parameterization is leveraged to construct policies for each agent, the policy parameters of each agent are shared with neighbors.

We hope that the above answers can clarify your doubts about using partial sharing.

**List References:**

* [Zhang et al., 2018] Fully decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning with networked agents. ICML, 2018.
* [Chen et al., 2021] Sample and communication-efficient decentralized actor-critic algorithms with finite-time analysis. arXiv 2021.
* [Arivazhagan et al., 2019] Federated learning with personalization layers. arXiv 2019.
* [Yu et al., 2020] Meta-world: A benchmark and evaluation for multi-task and meta reinforcement learning. CoRL, 2020.
* [Wai et al., 2018] Multi-agent reinforcement learning via double averaging primal-dual optimization. NeurIPS 2018.
* [Doan et al., 2019] Finite-time analysis of distributed TD (0) with linear function approximation on multi-agent reinforcement learning. ICML 2019.

content.title: Response Continued: Contributions and Clarifications
content.comment:
**Your comment: Lastly, there are a few restrictive assumptions in the paper. Though the references are convincing enough of the idea that these assumptions are common in some other works, it would be nice to include a brief discussion on the implications of these assumptions i.e. when will they hold true or be violated.**

**Our response:** Thanks for your question. We have revised our paper to present the following discussion after Assumption 4.


The main assumptions include: 
* observability in global state and global actions; 
* leveraging linear function approximation to parameterize global reward functions and global value functions; 
* full rank in feature matrices.

For MDP with linear dynamics and linear rewards, the linear function approximation is an appropriate choice. Then, with the assumptions above and under any fixed policy, there is a unique optimal solution for leveraging linear function to approximate global reward functions and global value functions. For actor-critic methods, It is crucial to have this property when developing the convergence analysis of policy parameters. 

However, it may be not suitable to use linear function approximation for complex MDP where the reward function is not linear anymore. If there is redundancy in the feature matrices and data features are not linearly independent, the full rank assumption is violated. Moreover, when the global observability assumption is violated and the MARL setting is considered in a partially observable Markov decision process, then the problem is much more challenging and finite sample complexity will not be guaranteed.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a coordinated actor-critic (CAC) algorithm for MARL with a shared part and an individual part. The shared part takes care of the homogeneity and is jointly optimized among all agents and a personalized part targets the heterogeneity among agents and is only locally optimized. Sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-5/2})$ is proved for the proposed CAC algorithm.
content.main_review:
The paper is well written and easy to follow. I checked the proof and I believe the main results are correct.

However, I have some major concerns regarding the motivation for separated joint policy and local policy, as well as how an agent could know which parts of his/her policy parameters are for the joint policy parameters or for the individual policy parameters. I am happy to raise my score if the following questions could be addressed.
(1) It is not clear to me what problem formulation (i.e., reward design and transition kernel) will lead to an optimal policy with a shared part and an individual part.

(2) At the beginning of Section 3.1, the authors assume directly the policy is decomposed into $\theta_i:=(\theta_i^s,\theta_i^p)$. This assumption is too strong from a practical perspective. Suppose a learning agent is optimizing over a 4-dimensional parameter space $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3,\theta_4)\in \mathbb{R}^4$. Why is it innocent to assume that the agent *knows a priori* that  (for example) $(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3)$ is for the shared policy and $\theta_4$ is for the local policy?

(3) In formulation (5), the authors restrict $\theta_i^s=\theta_j^s$ if (i,j) are neighbors. Does this imply that there are k global policies if there are k clusters on the graph? I don't feel the constraint is well motivated.

(4) It is stated on page 5 (under paragraph "Policy Optimization") that "trying to make sure that the shared parameters are not too fr from their neighbors". Again, if there exists strong heterogeneous behavior between two connected agents, then there is no incentive for them to take similar policy parameters.


Some other comments:

(a) The agents are assumed to have a joint state. Is it possible to have individual state space? If yes, does the complexity grow exponentially with respect to the number of agents?

(b) The authors consider linear function approximation for the reward. Can the authors say anything about the approximation error? See 
(Provably Efficient Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation, Chi et. al, 2019)

(c) Some references that might be relevant: 

Networked agents:

Scalable Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Agent Networked Systems (Qu et. al, 2019)

Mean-field regime:

A Principled Permutation Invariant Approach to Mean-Field Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (Li et. al, 2021)

Model-Free Mean-Field Reinforcement Learning: Mean-Field MDP and Mean-Field Q-Learning (Carmona et. al, 2019)

Mean-Field Controls with Q-learning for Cooperative MARL: Convergence and Complexity Analysis (Gu et. al, 2020)

MARL with shared policy:

Calibration of Shared Equilibria in General Sum Partially Observable Markov Games (Vadori et al, 2020)
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is well written and easy to follow. I checked the proof and I believe the main results are correct. However, I am not fully convinced why it is interesting or important to consider separated joint policy and local policy.

content.title: Response: Contributions and Clarifications
content.comment:
We appreciate your review and the positive comments regarding our paper. We would like to respond to your comments and hope that we address all your concerns below:

**Q1: It is not clear to me what problem formulation (i.e., reward design and transition kernel) will lead to an optimal policy with a shared part and an individual part.**

**Q2: At the beginning of Section 3.1, the authors assume directly the policy is decomposed into $\theta_i = (\theta_i^s, \theta_i^p)$. This assumption is too strong from a practical perspective. Suppose a learning agent is optimizing over a 4-dimensional parameter space 
$\theta = ( \theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3, \theta_4 ) \in \mathbb{R}^4$. Why is it innocent to assume that the agent knows a priori that (for example) $(\theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3)$ is for the shared policy and $\theta_4$ is for the local policy?**

**Our response:** Thank you for your comment. To answer Q1 and Q2 about *why* and *when* to use the partial policy sharing, we provide the following response:

(1) On the one hand, we use the partial policy sharing as a generic setting, to cover the full spectrum of strategies ranging from no sharing to full sharing. Therefore, to partially address Question 1 above, we are not saying that partial sharing must be the best strategy for any scenarios. Rather, *if* it happens to be a good strategy for *some* problems, then our algorithms and analysis can be directly used. To partially address Question 2, using the notation θ_i:=(θ_i^s, θ_i^p) is also for generality, so our subsequent analysis covers all three different cases. 

  On the other hand, note that, in our considered MARL setting, both the “full-sharing” and the “no-sharing” settings are important. The no sharing setting has been considered in [Zhang et al, 18] but there is no finite sample analysis. The full-sharing case is important when the agents’ tasks are similar. To the best of our knowledge, there has been no finite sample analysis and algorithm available for the full sharing case, and our work fills this gap. In addition, we found a concurrent work [Communication-Efficient Actor-Critic Methods for Homogeneous Markov Games] also submitted to ICLR 2022, which considers the fully shared case of decentralized AC algorithms for homogeneous Markov games and theoretically justifies the use of fully shared policy in the case of permutation-invariant multi-agent MDP. When the agents are homogeneous, the full parameter sharing scheme could actually leverage more data, which is collected from all agents, to update each local model. 

Please also refer to our response to Review 1, Question 1 for more detailed discussion on how to compare our contribution to the literature.

(2) As the reviewer mentioned, the agents may not know a *priori* how to partition the policy. In that case, the agents can choose to adopt either the full sharing or no sharing setting. However, in cases where there is a system planner (say, a game designer) who has the power to adjust the system setting before interaction starts, then the planner could use the domain knowledge about the system (such as whether the local tasks are similar), to set up how the agents may partially share their parameters. 

(3) Partial policy sharing has been proven useful in a few popular settings; for example the personalized federated learning and the multi-task RL setting mentioned in the paper. Generally speaking, partial sharing is useful when local tasks / agents share some similarity. But it is true that besides the above intuition, there is no definite answer as to *when* to use the partial sharing. 
Further, in practice, when partial sharing is used, it is typically found useful to construct neural networks where the parameters of base layers (first few layers) are shared among different agents and the parameters of personalization layers (last few layers) are locally optimized for adapting to the statistical heterogeneity of the local tasks.

content.comment:
(4) To further understand {\it when} and {\it how} to use partial sharing, below we provide a few examples, including some additional experiments we have done. 

In [Arivazhagan et al., 2019], a federated learning algorithm is developed to train the base layers (first few layers) through using existing decentralized optimization techniques to learn the similarities among different local datasets. Moreover, the personalization layers (last few layers) are trained locally to enable the neural network models to capture personalization information of local agents.

In [Yu et al., 2020], a multi-headed policy with one head per task is trained by the soft actor-critic algorithm in multi-task reinforcement learning environments. The policy is constructed by a neural network where the base layers are shared among different tasks and the personalized layers (heads) will adapt to each individual task.

To further evaluate the benefit of (partial) policy sharing, we have updated our paper by: 1) comparing the performance of CAC with benchmarks, for our pursuit-evasion game;  2) including one more experiment  (i.e., the coordination game) and compare CAC with a few benchmarks; please see Section 5 “Numerical Results”, the blue parts. 

We compare our algorithm CAC with independent AC, decentralized AC [Zhang et al., 2018] and the concurrent work mini-batch decentralized AC [Chen et al., 2021] mentioned above. In the coordination game, we show that compared with existing decentralized algorithms without policy sharing, CAC algorithm provides faster convergence and has larger chances of converging to efficient equilibriums due to the benefit of policy sharing. In the pursuit-evasion game, we show CAC algorithm could achieve the fastest convergence speed compared with the benchmarks.

**Q3: In formulation (5), the authors restrict $ \theta_i^s = \theta_j^s $if (i,j) are neighbors. Does this imply that there are k global policies if there are k clusters on the graph? I don't feel the constraint is well motivated.**

**Our response:** Thank you for your comment. Please note that a key assumption we made in Assumption 1, is that the union of any B consecutive graphs will be fully connected. That is, the graph will be connected infinitely often. In either way, there will not be k clusters on the graph, and there will be a single global policy. Note that such a connectedness assumption is a key to our analysis. 

On the other hand, suppose that the agents are connected by fixed but *unconnected* graphs. Since there is no communication among the clusters, then we cannot expect that the policy generated by different clusters of agents will be the same. That is, as the reviewer mentioned, in  this case there will be a number of different global policies. However, please note that our algorithm and analysis still applies, but not for the entire system, rather,  for each individual cluster of agents. 

**Q4: It is stated on page 5 (under paragraph "Policy Optimization") that "trying to make sure that the shared parameters are not too fr from their neighbors". Again, if there exists strong heterogeneous behavior between two connected agents, then there is no incentive for them to take similar policy parameters.**

**Our response:** This question is related to *why* we want to use the partial policy sharing in our model. In addition to our comments to your first question, we briefly explain again below.

We can view partial policy sharing as a *generic model*, to model all the possibilities from full sharing to non-sharing. Therefore, our algorithm, as well as the analysis, applies for all settings. For example, if, as the reviewer mentioned, there is strong heterogeneity and there is no need to share, then the system designer can inform the agents at the beginning, and they will run our algorithm (with $\theta^s =\emptyset$), and all the theoretical analysis still applies. Similarly, if there is strong homogeneity like homogeneous Markov games, then the algorithm can be run by setting $\theta^p= \emptyset$. In practice, the most common use of our algorithm is when local tasks / agents share both similarity and statistical heterogeneity in the multi-agent system. 

**Listed References:**

* [Zhang et al., 2018] Fully decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning with networked agents. ICML, 2018.
* [Chen et al., 2021] Sample and communication-efficient decentralized actor-critic algorithms with finite-time analysis. arXiv 2021.
* [Arivazhagan et al., 2019] Federated learning with personalization layers. arXiv 2019.
* [Yu et al., 2020] Meta-world: A benchmark and evaluation for multi-task and meta reinforcement learning. CoRL, 2020.
* [Grosnit et al., 2021] Decentralized Deterministic Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning. arXiv 2021.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) in a setting where all agents work cooperatively to maximize their average reward. Specifically, the global state $s$ is observable to all agents, and each agent has its own local action $a_i$. The agents can communicate over a time-varying network. The authors allow each agent to have a partially personalized policy $\theta_i$. For each agent $i$, a subset of parameters $\theta_i^s$ are shared among all agents, while the remaining part $\theta_i^p$ is optimized locally. The authors propose an actor-critic algorithm to optimize the policies, and analyze the number of samples needed to converge to a stationary point of the objective. Their results provide the first finite-time convergence bound that works for partially personalized policies in this MARL setting.
content.main_review:
The main contribution of this paper is the proposed Coordinated Actor-Critic (CAC) algorithm and its finite-time convergence bounds. However, since the framework of the proposed algorithm is similar with [Zhang et al., 2018], and many finite-time bounds exist in similar MARL settings, I think this contribution is not significant enough. Although the authors emphasize a major difference is that they allow a part of local policy parameters to be shared among all agents, I am not fully convinced about the importance of this generalization in policy class compared with fully personalized policies or fully shared policies. The advantage of CAC with partially shared parameters is only weakly demonstrated in the experiment part, and there are no theoretical results to guarantee that sharing a subset of parameters helps in homogeneous settings.

I might overlook some contributions of this work due to lack of familiarity. I hope the authors can help me understand the following questions better in the rebuttal:
1.	When the policy parameters in the proposed CAC algorithm is fully personalized or fully shared, are there any existing finite-time results for the same algorithm? Does the $O(\epsilon^{-\frac{5}{2}})$ sample complexity bound matches the best existing bounds in this MARL setting?
2.	How well does CAC compare with other benchmarks (excepts its variants) in numerical experiments? 
3.	This paper uses a linear function approximation for the global reward function. I don’t think this is common in previous works. Is there any justification for this approach?

Based on my current evaluation of this work, I will vote for weak reject with a low confidence score. I’m happy to adjust the score based on the authors’ response.

We appreciate your review and the positive comments regarding our paper. We would like to respond to your comments and hope that we address all your concerns below:

**Q1: When the policy parameters in the proposed CAC algorithm is fully personalized or fully shared, are there any existing finite-time results for the same algorithm? Does the $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-\frac{5}{2}})$ sample complexity bound matches the best existing bounds in this MARL setting?**

**Our response:** When the policy is fully personalized, the setting is the same as the cooperative MARL system introduced in [Zhang et al., 2018]. Although there have been a few variants, to our knowledge, there is no finite-time analysis before our work. After the submission of this work, we found that there is a concurrent work [Chen et al., 2021], also submitted to ICLR 2022, which also has a finite-sample analysis, but uses a different update strategy (to be discussed shortly in this response). 

When the policy is fully shared, the setting is new in the context of MARL. To our knowledge there is no finite sample analysis. We notice that there is a concurrent work [*Communication-Efficient Actor-Critic Methods for Homogeneous Markov Games*] also submitted to ICLR 2022, which considers the fully shared case of decentralized actor-critic algorithm for homogeneous Markov games. But the focus of their paper is very different in that they aim to quantify the optimality loss of searching fully shared policy and prove asymptotic convergence. 

Regarding the centralized algorithms, first, note that our finite sample analysis matches the results in [Wu et al., 2020] which established the $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{−\frac{5}{2}})$ sample complexity for two-timescale AC method in single-agent setting. Second, there is a recent line of work that shows that a variant of single-agent AC can achieve $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{−2})$ complexity; see [Xu et al., 2020]. However, unlike the standard two-timescale AC algorithm, this algorithm requires large-batch samples / inner loops to perform TD steps before updating the actor each time. [Chen et al., 2021] mentioned in the previous paragraph extends this work to the decentralized MARL setting. To be specific, $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{−1} \ln{\epsilon^{-1}} )$ samples need to be generated to update critic parameter before performing each actor update. While simple to analyze, these algorithms are not efficient in practice. In experiments, it can be observed that this large-batch variant may suffer from a poor sample complexity for the policy evaluation problem; further, since the agents need to wait a very long time between two policy updates (to collect enough samples for critics update), the policy is optimized very slowly. In our revised version, we include the comparison with this large-batch algorithm in numerical experiments. Compared with the large-batch versions, our proposed algorithm could provide better performance in terms of faster convergence speed and higher average reward in the MARL system.

**Q2:  How well does CAC compare with other benchmarks (excepts its variants) in numerical experiments?**

**Our response:** To address your question, we have updated our paper by: 1) comparing the performance of CAC with benchmarks, for our pursuit-evasion game;  2) including one more experiment  (i.e., the coordination game) where we compare CAC with a few benchmarks; please see the blue parts in Section 5. 

More specifically, We compare our algorithm CAC with independent AC, decentralized AC [Zhang et al., 2018] and the concurrent work mini-batch decentralized AC [Chen et al., 2021] mentioned above. In the coordination game, we show that CAC provides faster convergence and has larger chances of converging to efficient equilibriums due to the benefit of policy sharing. In the pursuit-evasion game, we show CAC could achieve the fastest convergence speed compared with the benchmarks.

**Q3: This paper uses a linear function approximation for the global reward function. I don’t think this is common in previous works. Is there any justification for this approach?**

**Our response:** Thank you for your comment. Note that to our knowledge, most of the state-of-the-art works on decentralized MARL with provable convergence guarantees utilizes the linear function approximation to estimate global advantage functions for update policy parameters. For example, in [Zhang et al., 2018] and [Grosnit et al., 2021], the global reward function and value function are approximated by linear functions and the global advantage function is estimated as $\hat{r}(s_t, a_t) + \gamma * \hat{V}(s_{t+1}) - \hat{V}(s_{t})$.

content.title: Clarification about my last question
content.comment: Thanks for the response! I think the authors misunderstood my last question. I mean why do you need to assume the reward can be approximated by $\hat{r}(s, a; \lambda) = \phi(s, a)^T \lambda$? I'm not sure this is common and necessary. Can you provide some references and/or justification? Thanks.

replying_to: Replying to Clarification about my last question

content.title: Response to the follow-up question
content.comment:
Thank you for your follow-up question! 

In fact, there are many previous works where the global reward is approximated as $\hat{r}(s,a; \lambda) = \phi(s,a)^T \lambda$. For example, in equations (3.9) - (3.11) of [Zhang et al., 2018] (http://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/zhang18n/zhang18n.pdf) and in equations (7) - (9) of [Grosnit et al., 2021] (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.09745.pdf), the authors utilize the same subroutine to approximate and update the global reward function as equation (12) in our paper.

Regarding the necessity of this approximation, note that in order to update the policy parameters towards maximizing the global objective, it is necessary to estimate the global advantage function $r(s_t, a_t) + \gamma * V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)$. There are two alternative ways to estimate the global advantage function:
* In [Zhang et al., 2018] and [Grosnit et al., 2021], the global advantage function is estimated by $\hat{r}(s_t,a_t) + \gamma * \hat{V}(s_{t+1}) - \hat{V}(s_{t})$ where the global reward function is approximated by $\hat{r}(s,a; \lambda) = \phi(s,a)^T \lambda$. Then [Zhang et al., 2018] and [Grosnit et al., 2021] utilize this estimator of the global advantage function to perform policy optimization steps for updating their policy parameters.

* In [Lin et al., 2019] and [Chen et al. 2021], the global advantage function is alternatively estimated by $\hat{Q}(s_t, a_t) - \hat{V}(s_{t})$ where the global Q function is approximated by $\hat{Q}(s,a; \omega) = \phi(s,a)^T \omega$. 

Either of these two approximation schemes is common in the literature of decentralized actor-critic methods. In our paper, we utilize the first scheme which needs to approximate the global reward function by linear functions.

Note that this is different from decentralized policy evaluation problems ([Wai et al., 2018] and [Doan et al., 2019]), which are simpler compared with decentralized actor-critic methods. In that case, it is appropriate to utilize $r_i + \gamma * \hat{V}(s_{t+1}) - \hat{V}(s_{t})$ to estimate the global TD error for updating parameters in value function approximators. This is because a fully mixing step is performed each time to aggregate the parameters in value function approximators. However, in decentralized actor-critic methods, when policy is partial-sharing or non-sharing, we should utilize the approximated global reward $\hat{r}(s,a; \lambda) = \phi(s,a)^T \lambda$ when updating the policy parameters since no fully mixing step is performed to aggregate all policy parameters.

We hope this response could address your question. Thank you very much!

**References:**
* [Zhang et al., 2018] Fully decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning with networked agents. ICML, 2018.
* [Grosnit et al., 2021] Decentralized Deterministic Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning. arXiv 2021.
* [Chen et al., 2021] Sample and communication-efficient decentralized actor-critic algorithms with finite-time analysis. arXiv 2021.
* [Lin et al., 2019] A communication-efficient multi-agent actor-critic algorithm for distributed reinforcement learning. IEEE CDC 2019.
* [Wai et al., 2018] Multi-agent reinforcement learning via double averaging primal-dual optimization. NeurIPS 2018.
* [Doan et al., 2019] Finite-time analysis of distributed TD (0) with linear function approximation on multi-agent reinforcement learning. ICML 2019.
